title: Micro-negotiation scaffold and clause-bundle strategy
content:
Purpose: quick, portable scaffold for 10–15 minute negotiation touchpoints (AE + legal + SE). Not a full playbook — focused on how to bundle related clauses into single concession vectors and micro-scripts for customer calls.

Why this helps:
- Keeps meetings focused: one concession vector = one trade. Avoids ad-hoc clause-by-clause drift.
- Speeds decisions for small-to-mid deals where full redline cycles are expensive.
- Helps AEs present tradeoffs in business terms.

Clause-bundle taxonomy (high-level):
1) Safety bundle: indemnity cap, limitation of liability, carve-outs for gross negligence/fraud, regulatory compliance clause.
2) Data-residency bundle: residency commitments, export controls, logging/audit access, subprocessor list + notification cadence.
3) Availability/ops bundle: SLA, credits, scheduled maintenance windows, incident notification SLAs, escalation contacts.
4) IP/outputs bundle: model-output IP, derivative rights, license-back, embedding retention rules.
5) Security/ops bundle (for Private): key management, network isolation, customer-managed keys, air-gap support.

Prioritization heuristic (for a 30min AE call):
- Start: identify which bundle is deal-stopping for customer (ask directly: "is there any single item that would block procurement?").
- If Safety or Data-residency = blocker, escalate to legal immediately; leave OPS details as post-signing SOW items if needed.
- If only availability or minor IP tweaks: propose commercial (term/price) trade instead of deep legal churn.

Micro-scripts (quick lines to use on calls):
- When customer asks for unlimited liability: "We can accept tailored liability for proven gross negligence or fraud but we typically cap at a mutually agreed multiple of fees — what exposure level is your procurement team expecting so I can bring a concrete proposal?"
- On data residency demands for hosted API: "We operate regionally and can commit to auth-bound region routing for production keys; for stronger residency guarantees we can discuss Dedicated or Private deployments and associated timeline/costs. Is timeline or control the bigger driver?"
- If asked to remove indemnity carve-outs: "Removing carve-outs would expose us to claims unrelated to Redwood's conduct and would require a pricing/insurance conversation — would the counterparty consider a tailored carve-out rather than wholesale removal?"

Sample minimal redline snippets (drop-in lines):
- Liability cap (balanced): "Except for liability arising from gross negligence, willful misconduct, or infringement indemnities, each party's aggregate liability shall not exceed the fees paid under this Agreement in the 12 months prior to the claim."
- Data residency (hosted fallback): "Redwood will make commercially reasonable efforts to route Customer production data to the Customer's selected geographic region and will provide a written plan for cross-border transfers on request."
- Model output IP (safe default): "Customer retains rights to outputs it supplies to or receives from the Service; Redwood retains rights to model weights and service improvements derived from aggregated telemetry, provided no Customer-identifying data is used."

Concession ladder (what to give vs get):
- Give: limited exceptions to SLA credits, reasonable list of subprocessor notices, minor SLAs for backups.
- Ask: a higher fee for Private/Dedicated options, a 12-month minimum for dedicated capacity, security questionnaires to be completed prior to onboarding.

Signals and red flags to watch in a call:
- Red flag: customer pushes for unlimited liability or removes carve-outs without a corresponding commercial concession. Put a hard pause and escalate.
- Flag: procurement requests full audit access to Redwood production environment. That is a Do Not Approve without SRE + infra involvement; offer logs and attestation instead.
- Positive signal: customer willing to accept a limited escrow or a short SOC2 review window — opens path to Private.

Escalation ladder (fast path):
1) AE notes top bundle blocker and posts brief to #legal-quick (template below)
2) If blocker = indemnity/liability or data residency that cannot be met by hosted routing, ping Legal SLA on-call and book 30min sync
3) If Private/Dedicated needed, involve Solutions Eng + Pricing for T&Cs and timeline

#legal-quick post template (one-liner + attachments):
- Deal: <ACV> / Customer: <name> / Bundle blocker: <safety|residency|ops|ip> / Requested change: <short phrase> / Desired response time: <24/48h>
- Attach: redline excerpt, security questionnaire PDF, procurement email thread link

Open questions (TODO):
- How firm is leadership on the 12-month fee lookback for cap calculation? (ask Jonah)
- Decision threshold for making a hosted region SLA binding vs "commercially reasonable efforts" language — get SRE input for latency/regional routing guarantees.
- Standard fallback wording for model telemetry derived improvements (privacy-safe language).

Quick checklist for a micro-call (AE + legal on 15min):
- 1m: AE frames the customer's blocker and desired business outcome
- 6m: Legal triage: which bundle(s) affected, quick yes/no on core carve-outs
- 6m: Offer 1–2 trade options (e.g., accept limited change in exchange for higher fee or a 12-month commit)
- 2m: Agree next steps or signpost escalation owner

Notes-to-self: keep this doc lean — convert commonly used micro-scripts into keyboard snippets in Google Docs and add to AE playbook. After next 3 deals, capture two real examples and the final language used (for precedent library).

Examples to add (post-call): record deal id, final concession given, who signed off (legal + exec), and whether change required infra work.

End.
